chunks: Other jobs of a ground plane. The question: In addition to providing a common reference potential, what are some other functionalities of ground planes?
A ground plane does much more than serve as zero volts. It is the return path for signals, which keeps loops small.

It sets the impedance of the traces above it, shields layers from each other, adds capacitance with a power plane, spreads heat, gives static-discharge current an easy path, balances the copper so the board stays flat, and acts as the other half of an antenna.
Cutting the plane weakens every one of these jobs.
Think of a Swiss army knife: one tool, many uses. Each of the plane's jobs uses a different property of one large copper sheet.
A knife with a snapped blade loses only that function. A plane with a slot cut in it loses several functions at once, because all its jobs depend on it staying continuous.

One plane, many jobs: signal return and fields (return path, impedance, shielding, EMI), power integrity (decoupling), and the jobs that just need a big conductor (heat spreading, ESD; mechanical balance and antenna counterpoise are covered below).
All of them depend on the plane staying continuous.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source, directly under the trace at high frequency ("Which layers should be ground").
Controlled impedance: a trace built to a set ratio of voltage to current for fast signals, which needs a plane beneath it ("Layers for high-speed signal routing").
Shielding: keeping fields from one circuit out of another ("Why a ground plane shields signals").
ESD (electrostatic discharge): a sudden spark of static current, like the zap from a doorknob. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current.
A fast current change through it creates a voltage.
Take ESD. A standard 8 kilovolts test spark delivers about 30 amps, rising in about 0. 8 nanoseconds. That is about 37. 5 amps per nanosecond.
The voltage across a ground connection is L di over dt , inductance times the rate of change. With 1 nanohenries of inductance it is about 38 volts.
With 5 nanohenries of thin trace, about 188 volts. A via right at the protection part keeps the spike small. For the antenna job, a quarter-wave antenna at 2.
4 gigahertz is about 31 mm long and needs a ground sheet to work against. That is the whole idea.

"Beyond being the reference, a ground plane is the return path that keeps loops small, so it cuts radiation, pickup and crosstalk; it defines trace impedance; it shields between layers; next to a power plane it adds high-frequency decoupling capacitance; it spreads heat; it gives ESD and surge currents a low-inductance path; it balances copper to limit warp; and it's the counterpoise for antennas.
Cutting it up gives up all of those at once."
Quick check. Which of these is NOT a typical function of a ground plane?
